analysis.one_liner: Requires an independent government audit of the Federal Reserve, including its monetary policy decisions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote in the two-year Congress and died in the Banking Committee with 8 Republican backers.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders the Government Accountability Office — Congress's independent audit agency — to conduct a full audit of the Federal Reserve Board and the 12 regional Federal Reserve banks within 12 months and report the findings to Congress. Today's law lets the GAO audit the Fed's bookkeeping but forbids it from reviewing the Fed's monetary policy decisions, its interest-rate deliberations, and its emergency lending. This bill strikes that exception, so the GAO could examine what the Fed decided, how it decided it, and who benefited from its transactions. Nothing in the bill changes how the Fed operates; it only opens the Fed's records to outside inspection.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want to know how monetary policy and Fed lending decisions are made. Under current law, the Fed's monetary deliberations and many of its transactions are exempt from audit by the GAO, and its audited financial statements are the only outside check. A full audit would let Congress and the public see whether Fed decisions — on interest rates, emergency lending, and international transactions — favored particular banks or counterparties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters seeking visibility into Fed decisions

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Comptroller General to complete a full audit of the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve banks within 12 months of enactment and report the findings to Congress within 90 days.

Repeals the provision of federal law (31 U.S.C. 714(b)) that exempts Federal Reserve monetary policy deliberations, decisions, and actions from GAO audit, allowing audit of international financial transactions, monetary policy matters, Federal Open Market Committee transactions, and internal Fed communications about them.

Replaces the existing narrow definition of auditable emergency facilities with a broad one covering any program or facility established by the Board or a Reserve bank under its emergency lending authority, so such programs cannot stay outside the audit.

analysis.who_pays: The Federal Reserve and the large banks that deal with it bear the costs: auditors scrutinizing rate deliberations and emergency lending could expose individual banks' borrowing, and the Fed loses a layer of discretion shielded from congressional review. Taxpayers pay for the GAO audit itself, a modest cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Federal Reserve and large banks

drawbacks.text: Opening the Fed's monetary policy deliberations to audit by a congressional agency could expose rate-setting discussions to political pressure. The Fed's independence from day-to-day politics is the reason many economists give for its credibility on inflation, and auditors second-guessing rate decisions could erode it.

The bill requires audit of Fed 'discussions and communications' about monetary policy. If Fed officers know their internal debates could be reviewed and reported, they may hesitate to speak candidly, and public release of emergency-lending details during a crisis could make banks avoid Fed support when the economy most needs them to use it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: an outside audit of an institution that sets the price of credit for every household, with no other outside review of its decisions. The cost is the risk that political scrutiny of rate deliberations makes monetary policy worse or freezes Fed lending in a crisis — a risk opponents have weighed against the transparency gain in every Congress this proposal has appeared. The bill does not force public disclosure of the audit's underlying materials to everyone; it reports to Congress, so the political pressure runs through legislators rather than headlines.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never reached the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the Federal Reserve Transparency Act of 2021 on March 3, 2021, with seven Republican cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
That was the only action the bill ever received; the committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Federal Reserve keeps the legal exemption that bars outside audit of its monetary decisions and emergency lending, and the banks that deal with it are spared a public audit trail. Members of Congress gain nothing to answer for, since no record of them acting on Fed transparency was ever created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Federal Reserve and its banking counterparties

against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which it could not reach without a committee vote anyway.

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters were Republicans; no Democrat or Independent cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled Banking Committee never acted.

industries.note: The bill strips the Fed's statutory exemption from GAO audit of its monetary decisions and emergency lending and requires a full audit. The Fed would lose discretion it has held since the 1970s, though the audit does not change its authority to set policy.

Banks that borrow from the Fed or benefit from its emergency programs would face audit scrutiny of those transactions, and visibility could make banks hesitant to use Fed support in a crisis — which can amplify downturns. At the same time, an audit could expose any instance of Fed lending that favored particular institutions.
